text: A mystery attending the disappearance of a Chinese woman and a child on February 17 was solved yesterday when the bodies were found on the hillside at Pokfulam.

label: paragraph_title
text: BODIES OF MOTHER AND CHILD FOUND.

label: text
text: The woman was lying on her back with the child underneath her. It is thought that he was sitting with the child strapped to her back when she fell back and died. There were no marks of violence on the body.

label: text
text: In the House of Commons the Marquess of Hartington (Conservative, West Derbyshire) asked whether communications had been received from the Dominions expressing their views on the proposed increase in the permanent membership of the League of Nations Council?

label: text
text: Mr. L. S. Amary, Secretary, of State for the Dominions, referred to Sir Austen Chamberlain's reply on February 17. He added that it was impossible to make a statement as to the nature of such communications which were of a confidential character.

label: text
text: Mr. J. H. Thomas (Labour, Derby) requested that the correspondence be submitted to the House before there was any debate.

label: text
text: Mr. Amery replied that he was not sure that he would be able to do so. He said that it would largely depend on the views of the Dominion Governments concerned.

label: text
text: Mr. Thomas asked if it was not essential that the House should know exactly the Dominion view-point before, the debate?

label: text
text: The anxiety of the members of the House of Commons on the League Council issue was reflected in questions by three Liberals and one Conservative asking whether a decision had been reached as regards the instructions to Sir Austen Chamberlain at Geneva and whether the Dominions would be consulted before Great Britain was committed to any change?

label: text
text: Mr. Stanley Baldwin (Prime Minister) in a joint reply requested the House to await a statement which he hoped to make later in the week, probably on Thursday.

label: text
text: Mr. J. Ramsay MacDonald (Labour leader) requested a statement on Wednesday.

label: text
text: The Prime Minister promised to his best.

label: text
text: Mr. Stanley Baldwin, Prime Minister, announced in the House of Commons that he hoped to be able to make a statement on Thursday, or perhaps Wednesday regarding the instructions to be given to the British delegates to the League of Nations Council on the question of the enlargement of the Council beyond the admission of Germany.

label: text
text: A number of questions was addressed to him on the subject, and he requested that these should be postponed until he was able to make his statement. If, on consideration, it should be thought desirable to have a brief discussion on that statement, the opportunity of doing so would be given.

label: text
text: The attention of Sir Austen Chamberlain, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, was called to the fact that the agenda of the League Council has been arranged so that the question of the Saar Commission will be brought up first before Germany has been admitted to the League.

label: text
text:
Sir A. Chamberlain was asked whether the Government would endeavour to secure that a matter so closely concerning German interests should be postponed until Germany can be represented?
Sir A. Chamberlain replied that it was the usual practice of the Council to decide matters relating to its procedure, and he had been unable to anticipate the Council's decision on this occasion. As to obtaining a postponement of the Saar question he did not think that the interests of peace and international understanding were served by members of individual Governments saying what they would or would not do at a meeting of that great world Council—the Council of the League—and he did not see how an agreed decision could ever be reached if any Government announced its policy beforehand and was unwilling to make concessions.

text: In the House of Commons, Mr. F. C. Penny (Conservative, Kingston-on-Thames), asked whether Cantonese Bolshevik elements in the Straits Settlements were engaging in propaganda and fomenting strikes, and whether the Chinese master-tailors in Singapore had petitioned the Governor (Sir Laurence Guillemard) to have the Tailors' Guild broken up and the ring-leaders deported?

label: text
text: Mr. L. S. Amery, Secretary of State for the Colonies, stated that the recent strikes had been economic. The reply to the second part of the question was in the affirmative, but the Governor had reported that the master tailors had not produced evidence in support of their allegations, consequently the deportations had not been effected. He declared that the Straits Government was closely watching the situation.

text: It remains to be seen whether the Government will accept the proposed compromise.

He declared that there was a real case for consideration on the composition of the Council. The demand that the practice of rejecting non-permanent members year after year should be abandoned was growing. He was immovably opposed to the suggestion that any State should be brought on the Council as a counterpoise to Germany, but there was a sound argument for increasing the permanent membership since under the Locarno Agreement possibly Germany and all the present permanent members, except Japan, would be regarded as interested parties and therefore unable to vote if a dispute under the Locarno Treaty were submitted to the Council.

label: text
text:
The question of how the Council could be made most effective for the maintenance of peace and conciliation was the real test. That ought to be applied not to any counting of votes in a body where, unless there was unanimity, there could be no decision.
Sir A. Chamberlain contended that if on great questions the British representatives were required to define their attitude unequivocably beforehand, the delegates of other Governments would be forced in the same position, and paralysis would result owing to one State vetoing one solution and another State vetoing another solution.
The only way to keep the door open for conciliatory negotiation was to avoid irrevocable commitments on the part of any delegate in advance. He hoped that complete harmony might be achieved through the preliminary conversations in the Logorno manner with the German delegates at Geneva. text: The engineering look-out has been brought a step nearer owing to a meeting of the strikers of the London firm of printing machine manufacturers, Robert Hoe & Co., which are the origin of the dispute, neumfirming their decision not to return to work.

label: text
text: Their attitude will be further discussed at a joint meeting of the Executives of the seven Unions involved when efforts will be made to avert a stoppage.

label: text
text: (A jobleghtm published in our columns on Saturday stated: The Engineering and Allied Employers' National Federation has decided to post lock-out notices on March 5, to be operative on March 13, in all federated establishments. In consequence of a strike by a section of London engineers and labourers over wageage and a refusal to work with non-Unionists. The Engineering Union refuses to recognise the strikers' action.)

label: text
text: It is expected that the French Minister of Finance, M. Doumer, will come to London next week to take up the negotiations with the Chapcélor of the Exchequer, Mr Winston Churchill, regarding France's war debt to Great Britain.

label: text
text:
The provisional agreement reached in last year's discussion between M. Caillaux (then French Minister of Finance) and Mr. Winston Churchill was on the basis of an average annual payment of £12,000,000.
Replying to a question on the French debt in the House of Commons last Thursday Mr. Winston Churchill said that the British Government regarded the bargain made with M. Caillaux as binding on both parties.

The Budget was presented in the Assembly today. It shows that the revenue for the past financial year was 131.35 crores of rupees and the expenditure 130.05 crores of rupees.
The Estimates for next year show the revenue to be 133.43 crores and the expenditure 130.88 crores.

label: text
text: There will be no fresh taxation. The repeal of the cotton excise duty would cost the Government 175 lakhs (a lakh equals 1,00,000 rupees).

label: text
text: Mir. L. S. Amery, Secretary of State for the Dominions and Colonies, was questioned in the House of Commons to-day regarding the agenda of the Imperial Conference which is to be held in London next October.

label: text
text: He replied that it was contemplated that there should be a discussion on questions of foreign policy and defence, including those arising out of the Locarno Treaty, and also of economic matters.

label: text
text:
In the House of Commons, to-day, Mr. Ronald F. McNeill, Financial Secretary to the Treasury, in moving a vote of £48,700 for salaries and expenses of the Imperial War Graves Commission, explained that last Summer all the Governments of the British Empire, including that of British India, had agreed to accumulate a fund until it should reach a capital sum which would provide in perpetuity an income sufficient to maintain the British war cemeteries in the different parts of the world in the manner that the nation desired that they should be £5,000,000, and it was estimated that the annual sum necessary would be from £200,000 to £250,000. It was in order to provide this country's first contribution that the Government asked the House to vote £50,000, less some small savings, for the purpose this year, and to vote the same sum for the next two years.
It was hoped that, at the end of 15 years, by the accumulation of the interest on these grants, with the contributions which would come from the Dominion Governments, the sum of £5,000,000 would be obtained.
